title: What Does a Benefits Broker Do?
summary: A benefits broker shops carriers, negotiates renewals, and handles compliance. Learn what a benefits broker does, how they get paid, and when you need one.
body_markdown:
Most founders and small business owners meet a benefits broker the week they realize they need to offer health insurance and have no idea where to start. I sit on the Warp Insurance Services Benefits team, and in the past three months alone, I've handled more than 300 employee onboardings, offboardings, and qualifying life events for dozens of startups. From setting up a brand-new five-person group in California to working the renewal for a 77-person company, I did some version of most of what's below this week.


And the question I hear most often is some version of, "What does a benefits broker actually do?"


## **What is a benefits broker?**


A benefits broker is a licensed intermediary between employers and insurance carriers. The license matters. In the United States, brokers are licensed by each state's department of insurance, and a broker can only sell in the states where they hold a license. That becomes important for businesses with employees in more than one state.


The broker's job is to translate. Carriers speak in plan designs, networks, and rate filings. Employers speak in budgets, headcount, and what their team actually needs. The broker sits between the two and makes sure the plan you buy fits the company you run.


## **What does a benefits broker do?**


The work falls into six areas. Some happen once a year, and some happen every week.


### **Shops the market**


A broker pulls quotes from multiple carriers and compares them side by side: premiums, deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums, and provider networks. A plan that looks cheap might not be a good deal if your team's doctors aren't in-network. The more carrier relationships a broker has, the more options you see.


### **Negotiates pricing and renewals**


Renewal is where having a broker pays off. Carriers send a renewal rate, and an engaged broker pushes back, remarkets the account, or restructures the plan so a rate increase does not land entirely on your budget or your employees. A broker who only shows up in the last two weeks before renewal is doing only a fraction of the job.


### **Handles enrollment and carrier administration**


Someone has to enroll every employee, add new hires, remove departures, and fix the inevitable mismatch between payroll deductions and carrier billing. A good broker or benefits team owns that work so your founder or office manager does not spend open enrollment in spreadsheets.


### **Keeps you compliant**


Offering benefits creates obligations. Companies with 50 or more full-time employees must offer coverage under the Affordable Care Act. Smaller companies that offer coverage still deal with plan documents, required notices, and state continuation rules. A broker flags these before they become penalties.


One we watch closely: once a client grows past 20 benefit-eligible employees, federal COBRA kicks in, and[every departing employee must receive a COBRA election notice](https://www.warp.co/blog/how-does-cobra-work-for-employers) . Fast-growing startups often cross that line without noticing, so we reach out when they do and line up a COBRA administrator before their next departure turns into a missed notice.


### **Supports employees**


When an employee gets a surprise bill or cannot find an in-network specialist, they should not have to wait on hold with a carrier. A broker or advisor who knows your specific plan can escalate directly with the insurer. This is the part of the job that employees remember.


### **Manages offboarding and COBRA**


When someone leaves, their coverage does not simply stop. COBRA continuation rules apply, and employers usually either manage COBRA themselves or rely on a carrier portal that does the bare minimum. Many brokers hand this off, so ask who will actually handle it before you sign.


## **How do benefits brokers get paid?**


There are three common models.


- **Carrier commission.** The carrier pays the broker, usually as a share of the premium you pay. The employer does not receive a separate invoice, which is why brokers often describe their services as "free." The cost is built into the premium.
- **Flat or hourly fee.** The employer pays the broker directly for advice and administration. This is more common with larger employers and consultants.
- **A mix of both.** Some brokers collect commission and charge an additional fee for extra services.


The tension in the commission model is that a broker's income can depend on which carrier you choose and how much you spend. That does not make commission-based brokers bad. It means you should ask directly.


Federal law now helps. Under the[Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/133/text) , brokers and consultants who expect to receive $1,000 or more in direct or indirect compensation for services to an employer's group health plan must disclose that compensation in writing to the plan fiduciary before the contract is entered into, extended, or renewed. The rules apply to contracts executed on or after December 27, 2021. The disclosure covers what services the broker provides, what they will be paid, and who is paying them. If a broker is vague about any of that, treat it as a signal.


## **Do you need a benefits broker?**


If you are offering group health coverage, almost always yes. You can technically buy a small group plan directly from a carrier, but you give up comparison shopping, renewal negotiation, and someone who knows your plan when claims go wrong. In most small group markets, the premium for a given plan is generally the same whether you buy through a broker or directly because rates are filed with the state, so a broker usually doesn't cost more.


There are cases where a traditional broker is not the right fit. If your team is spread across many states, a single small group plan may not work well, and an ICHRA, where you give each employee a tax-advantaged monthly allowance to buy their own plan, can be a better answer. We cover how that works in our guide to[ICHRA health insurance](https://www.warp.co/blog/ichra-health-insurance-for-startups) . Either way, someone still needs to advise you on the choice, which is also part of a broker's job.


## **What to look for in a benefits broker**


Before you sign with anyone, ask these questions:


- How will you be paid, by whom, and how much? Can I get the compensation disclosure in writing?
- Which carriers do you work with, and do any exclusive arrangements limit what you can show me?
- Who is my day-to-day contact, and what is the response time for employee questions?
- What do you do between renewals?
- Who handles COBRA, enrollment errors, and mid-year changes?
- Are you licensed in every state where I have employees?

## **FAQ**


### **How do benefits brokers make money?**


Most are paid a commission by the insurance carrier, built into the premium you already pay. Others charge a flat or hourly fee, and some do both. Under federal disclosure rules, brokers expected to earn $1,000 or more from a group health plan must tell the employer in writing how they are paid.


### **Is it cheaper to get health insurance through a broker?**


Usually it costs the same. In most small-group markets, the rate for a given plan is the same whether you buy through a broker or directly, so the broker's commission typically doesn't add to your cost. The savings come from finding a better-fit plan and negotiating renewals.


### **What is the downside of using a benefits broker?**


The main risk is misaligned incentives. A commission-paid broker may favor carriers that pay more or that they already work with, and some only engage at renewal. Ask how they are paid, which carriers they can show you, and what service looks like between renewals.


### **Do startups need a benefits broker?**


If you offer a group health plan, a broker is strongly recommended, even with fewer than 50 employees, when coverage is not legally required. If your team is spread across many states, an ICHRA may be a better fit, and a good advisor can help you decide.


### **What is the difference between a benefits broker and a benefits consultant?**


Brokers primarily procure and manage insurance for a commission, while consultants usually focus on broader benefits strategy for a fee. The line is blurry, and many firms do both, so ask any provider to spell out exactly what's included and what's not.
